newsitem.title: USA: Army Corps criticized for lack of wetlands appeals.
newsitem.headline: Army Corps criticized for lack of wetlands appeals.

text.p: The head of the House Natural Resources committee on Tuesday chastised the Army Corps of Engineers for failing to create an administrative appeals process as part of its management of sensitive wetlands.
"Too many (federal) agencies think that they are god," Rep. Don Young, a Republican from Alaska, said at a hearing of the committee's panel on water resources and environment.

"No one trusts you" to protect the nation's wetlands, Young said in questioning Michael Davis, a deputy assistant secretary of the Army. Young criticized the Army Corps of Engineers as slow to issue decisions on developers' applications for projects near wetlands.
Young also said the Corps of Engineers had failed to follow through on a congressional mandate to create an administrative appeals process for land developers denied permits.
Davis told the panel that the Corps had been unable to implement an appeals process because of budget cuts, but planned to do so in 1998.
"We'd like to go ahead with it," Davis said. "There have been a lot of accomplishments and the overall program is working better."

The National Association of Home Builders said at the hearing that illegal and unnecessary regulatory changes by the Corps of Engineers related to Nationwide Permit 26 added delays and costs to the construction of new homes. The permit gives builders an expedited permitting process, provided the project has a minimal impact on the environment. Environment groups oppose any relaxation of wetlands management, saying the destruction of wetlands by developers leaves homeowners vulnerable to flooding. A Sierra Club analysis said floods have killed nearly 500 people and destroyed $33 billion in homes and property over the past four years.

The hearing was held to discuss last December's reissurance of a nationwide permit program and a January federal court decision that invalidated the Corp of Engineers' excavation rule. An estimated 70,000 to 90,000 acres of wetlands is lost annually in the United States, for a total of some 100 million acres lost over the years, Davis said.

Several members of the subcommittee said they hoped to move forward quickly with more extensive wetlands protection under the Clean Water Act. Wetlands help recharge groundwater, control flooding and support commercial fishing and outdoor recreation.
"Congress has been indecisive on wetlands policy for far too long," said Rep. JoAnn Emerson, a Republican from Missouri. "We need a comprehensive, common-sense approach."
